name: n01-dnschain
title: The name resolution chain
spec: Vertical chain of seven numbered boxes top to bottom, arrows between them, a small 'answer found: stop here' side arrow leaving the /etc/hosts box. Boxes: 1 '/etc/nsswitch.conf (hosts: line sets the order)'; 2 '/etc/hosts (static overrides, no network traffic)'; 3 'stub resolver / local cache (127.0.0.53, systemd-resolved)'; 4 'search domains and ndots'; 5 'DNS query: UDP port 53 (TCP if truncated), A and AAAA'; 6 'recursive resolver: root, then .com, then example.com authoritative'; 7 'choose among answers: RFC 6724 order, Happy Eyeballs'. Monospace for file names and port. Orange highlight on box 2 side note 'a match ends the lookup'. Green main boxes. Bottom green bar: 'Each door can be locked and each fails differently'.
anchor: ## 3. Step 1: name resolution (what is the IP address?)
cap: The C library tries the files, the local stub or cache, the search domains and finally the recursive resolver, in order.

name: n01-curlw
title: Reading curl -w timing
spec: A horizontal timeline bar from left to right split into five segments, with six tick marks above labelled in order: namelookup, connect, appconnect (TLS done), pretransfer, starttransfer (first byte), total. Below each segment a bracket with its formula: 'DNS = namelookup'; 'TCP = connect minus namelookup'; 'TLS = appconnect minus connect'; 'request + server time + first byte = starttransfer minus pretransfer'; 'transfer = total minus starttransfer'. Tick labels in monospace as time_namelookup etc. Orange note: 'All values count from the start'. Green bar: 'Start with the largest phase, since that is where the time went'.
cap: Each curl -w value counts from zero, so each phase is the difference between two values.

name: n01-symptommap
title: From symptom to layer
spec: Left-to-right ladder of layers from bottom to top: Routing, ARP/ND, Transport, Name resolution, TLS/PKI, Application. Each layer is a row with a curl symptom chip and exit code: Name resolution: 'Could not resolve host' (exit 6); Routing: 'Network is unreachable' (exit 7); ARP/ND: 'No route to host' (exit 7); Transport: 'Connection refused' (exit 7, no listener), 'Connection timed out' (28/7, loss or firewall DROP); TLS/PKI: 'certificate verify failed' (60); Application: 'HTTP 4xx/5xx' (22 with -f). Orange highlight on the title note 'start with the layer the message points to'. Message text in monospace.
anchor: ## 12. A map from symptom to layer
alt: Curl error symptoms mapped to layers
cap: A curl error message and exit code point to the layer where you should start looking.

name: n02-switching
title: Circuit versus packet switching
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel 'Circuit switching': two endpoints joined by a single reserved path drawn as a solid thick line, notes: 'path and bandwidth reserved before data flows', 'predictable delay and jitter', 'bandwidth idle during silence'. Right panel 'Packet switching': data cut into packets, each with a header, travelling across a mesh of devices sharing links, notes: 'each packet carries a destination in its header', 'links used efficiently', 'queues can fill and packets get dropped'. Orange highlight on the bottom line: 'Ask first: does the network reserve a path or share one?'.
anchor: ## 1. Two ways to build a network
cap: Circuit switching reserves a path, while packet switching shares links and forwards each packet by its header.

name: n02-goodput
title: Overhead and goodput
spec: A stacked horizontal bar for one 1500-byte MTU segment, left to right, with byte counts: Preamble+gap 20 B (grey), Ethernet header 14 B, IP header 20 B, TCP header 20 B, data 1460 B (big green block), FCS 4 B. Label above: '1460 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 + 20 = 1538 byte times'. Below three result chips: 'MTU 1500: 1460 / 1538 = 94.9%', 'MTU 9000 (jumbo): 8960 / 9038 = 99.1%', 'Tiny 64-byte frame: 84 byte times on the wire, up to 148.8 million frames per second at 100 Gb/s' (orange). Monospace for arithmetic.
cap: Headers and gaps cost about 5 percent at 1500 bytes MTU and under 1 percent with jumbo frames.

name: n02-demux
title: Demultiplexing a frame
spec: Four stacked steps top to bottom with arrows, following one frame upward from the NIC: 'Ethernet: EtherType 0x0800 -> IPv4'; 'IPv4: protocol 6 -> TCP'; 'TCP: destination port 443 -> socket bound to port 443'. At the side a lookup table of keys: EtherType 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP, 0x8100 VLAN; IP protocol 1 ICMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP; ports 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 443 HTTPS, 4791 RoCE v2. Orange note: 'No handler matches: packet dropped, ICMP unreachable or TCP RST'. Monospace for hex values.
anchor: ### Demultiplexing: how the right code gets the bytes
cap: Each layer carries a key field that tells the receiver which code should get the payload next.

name: n02-planes
title: The three planes
spec: Three stacked horizontal bands labelled Management plane (top), Control plane (middle), Data (forwarding) plane (bottom). Each band has a job line and example chips. Management: 'configures and monitors' with SSH, REST APIs, Prometheus exporters, NETCONF/gNMI, syslog. Control: 'builds the tables' with OSPF, IS-IS, BGP, STP, ARP/ND, LACP. Data: 'moves packets at line rate: parse, lookup FIB, rewrite, queue, transmit' with switching, NAT, ACL matching. Arrow from Control labelled 'RIB best routes -> FIB' to Data. Orange note: 'What happens to traffic when the control plane fails?'.
cap: The data plane moves packets, the control plane builds the tables it uses, and the management plane configures and monitors.

name: n03-macbits
title: Anatomy of a MAC address
spec: A 6-octet strip: octets 1-3 'OUI (assigned by IEEE, names the vendor)' and octets 4-6 'NIC-specific (assigned by manufacturer)'. Zoom callout on octet 1 showing two bits: bit 0 (LSB) 'I/G: 0 = unicast, 1 = multicast or broadcast' and bit 1 'U/L: 0 = universally administered (burned-in), 1 = locally administered'. Side chips in monospace: 'ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff = broadcast', '01:00:5e:xx:xx:xx = IPv4 multicast mapping', '33:33:xx:xx:xx:xx = IPv6 multicast mapping'. Orange highlight on U/L bit with note 'virtual NICs often set it'.
cap: The first three octets name the vendor, and two bits of the first octet say unicast or multicast and burned-in or locally set.

name: n03-frame
title: The Ethernet frame
spec: One horizontal row of fields with byte widths: Preamble 7 B, SFD 1 B, Dest MAC 6 B, Src MAC 6 B, 802.1Q tag [4 B] (TPID 0x8100, PCP, DEI, VID) shown dashed as optional, EtherType 2 B, Payload (+pad) 46-1500 B, FCS 4 B (CRC-32), then 'inter-frame gap 12 B idle'. A bracket under Dest MAC to FCS: 'Ethernet frame: 64 to 1518 B (1522 B with VLAN tag)'. Orange highlight on Dest MAC with note 'arrives first: NIC decides at once whether to keep the frame'. Monospace for hex.
cap: Every Ethernet frame has the same field order, which lets a NIC decide in hardware.

name: n03-arp
title: ARP request and reply
spec: Two hosts and a switch. Host A (203.0.113.10) on the left, Host B (203.0.113.12) on the right, a third host C below. Step 1 arrow from A: 'ARP request, broadcast: who has 203.0.113.12? tell 203.0.113.10' reaching all hosts (dashed to C, solid to B). Step 2 arrow from B back to A: 'ARP reply, unicast: 203.0.113.12 is at B's MAC'. Beside it the 28-byte packet fields row: hardware type (Ethernet=1), protocol type (IPv4=0x0800), HLEN 6, PLEN 4, opcode (1=request, 2=reply), sender MAC, sender IP, target MAC (00:00:.. in request), target IP. Orange on target MAC '00:00:.. in request'. Monospace for IPs.
cap: An ARP request is broadcast to the whole segment, and the owner of the address answers with a unicast reply.

name: n03-ndp
title: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
spec: Three-step vertical sequence between a new host (left) and a router (right). Step 1: 'form link-local address fe80::/64 + interface ID'. Step 2: 'DAD: NS sent from :: for the address; any NA back means duplicate'. Step 3: 'RS (type 133) to ff02::2 -> RA (type 134): prefix, gateway lifetime, flags'; then 'SLAAC builds global address if A flag set; M flag = use DHCPv6'. Side table of ICMPv6 types: 133 RS, 134 RA, 135 NS (to solicited-node multicast ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX), 136 NA, 137 Redirect. Orange highlight on 'No broadcast: solicited-node multicast reaches only matching hosts'.
cap: A new IPv6 host builds a link-local address, checks it with DAD, then learns the prefix from a router advertisement.

name: n04-ipv6struct
title: Structure of an IPv6 address
spec: One long bar split into three segments: 'site prefix 48 bits' + 'subnet ID 16 bits' + 'interface ID 64 bits'. Beneath, the example 2001:0db8:0a0b | 12f0 | 0000:0000:0000:8b6e aligned to the segments (monospace). A bracket over the first two segments 'first 64 bits = the /64 subnet prefix'. Below, nested boxes: ISP/cloud /32 contains site /48 contains 65,536 /64 subnets. Orange note: 'Almost every subnet is a /64'.
cap: A global IPv6 address is a site prefix, a subnet ID and a 64-bit interface ID, and subnets are almost always /64.

name: n04-ipv6types
title: Reading IPv6 address prefixes
spec: Table with two columns, prefix (monospace) and meaning, rows: '::1/128' loopback; '2000::/3' global unicast (begins with 2 or 3); 'fd00::/8' unique local (ULA, private); 'fe80::/10' link-local, valid on one link only; 'ff00::/8' multicast (ff02::1 all nodes, ff02::2 all routers); '2001:db8::/32' documentation; '::ffff:0:0/96' IPv4-mapped; '64:ff9b::/96' NAT64. Orange highlight on the line 'There is no broadcast in IPv6'.
cap: The first digits of an IPv6 address tell you its type, and multicast replaces broadcast.

name: n04-ipv4hdr
title: The IPv4 header
spec: A 32-bit-wide grid, four columns of 8 bits, rows: Row1 Version | IHL | DSCP | ECN | Total Length; Row2 Identification | Flags | Fragment Offset; Row3 TTL | Protocol | Header Checksum; Row4 Source Address; Row5 Destination Address; Row6 Options (rare). Side notes: 'IHL 5 = 20 bytes', 'TTL drops by one at each router', 'Flags: DF and MF'. Orange highlight on Protocol with note '6 = TCP'. Monospace for field names.
cap: The IPv4 header is 20 bytes minimum, with fragmentation fields, TTL and a protocol field.

name: n05-rules
title: Which table gets consulted
spec: Vertical stack of three table cards in lookup order, top to bottom, with ip rule show priorities at left in monospace: '0: from all lookup local' -> table local (255): local and broadcast addresses, kernel maintained, consulted first; '32766: from all lookup main' -> table main (254): what ip route shows, connected, static, DHCP routes; '32767: from all lookup default' -> table default (253): usually empty. At the side an orange card: 'custom tables (1-252, 256+): one per NIC, tenant or VRF; a lower rule number means higher priority, and rules can match the source address'. Green main cards.
anchor: ## 3. Routing tables, rules and special routes
cap: Rules in ip rule decide which routing table the kernel looks in, starting with local, then main, then default.

name: n05-weakhost
title: Weak host model and asymmetric replies
spec: Diagram of a server with two NICs, NIC A (left, subnet A) and NIC B (right, subnet B), a client on subnet B at the bottom. Solid arrow: request arrives on NIC B addressed to B's address. Orange arrow: reply leaves through NIC A because the main table decides by destination. Orange red-cross note on the reply: 'rp_filter may drop it'. Side table rp_filter values in monospace: '0 no source validation', '1 strict: best route back must use same interface', '2 loose: source reachable via any interface'. Takeaway line: 'If the reply leaves on the wrong NIC, fix with policy routing before relaxing rp_filter'.
anchor: ## 5. Multiple interfaces: weak host model, rp_filter and asymmetric routing
alt: Weak host model with two NICs
cap: Linux routes replies by destination only, so a reply can leave on a different NIC than the request arrived on.

name: n05-ecmp
title: ECMP route on a host
spec: A host box on the left with two outgoing arrows to two next hops on the right: 'via 10.100.0.1 dev ens1f0 weight 1' and 'via 10.100.1.1 dev ens2f0 weight 1', both leading to a cloud labelled '10.200.0.0/16'. Below, table of net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy in monospace: 0 = L3 (src/dst IP), 1 = L4 (5-tuple), 2 = inner L3 for encapsulated, 3 = custom fields. Orange note: 'L3-only hashing: every connection between the same two hosts takes the same path (no port entropy)'.
cap: A multipath route has several equal-cost next hops, and the hash policy decides which packet details pick the path.

name: n05-sixnets
title: A GPU server with six networks
spec: Server box in the centre with three groups of NICs: eno1 -> management 10.20.0.0/24 (carries the default route, highlighted orange); eno2 -> storage 10.30.4.0/24 reaching NFS and Lustre servers at 10.30.0.0/16; ens1f0..ens8f0 -> eight RoCE rails each on 10.100.R.0/24 with no gateway. Beside the storage link the fix chip in monospace: '10.30.0.0/16 via 10.30.4.1 dev eno2'. Beside management: 'exactly one default route, on management'. Bottom green bar: 'Audit with ip route get <dst> from <src> in CI after provisioning'.
anchor: ## 12. Case study: a GPU server with six networks
cap: One default route on management, a static route for storage, and one subnet per rail keep each kind of traffic on its own NIC.

name: n06-window
title: The sliding window
spec: A long strip of byte numbers 1 to 40 drawn as cells, with a frame (window) sliding in three steps stacked vertically. Step 1: receiver advertises window 20; sender sends bytes 1 to 10. Step 2: receiver acknowledges 10 and advertises 30; sender may send up to byte 40, sends bytes 11 to 15. Step 3: receiver acknowledges 15 and advertises 40. Cells coloured: acknowledged (green), in flight (light), may send (outline). Orange note: 'If the application reads slowly the window shrinks to zero; sender sends window probes'. Footer: sender may have at most min(rwnd, cwnd) in flight.
cap: The window slides forward as ACKs arrive, letting the sender keep many segments in flight.

name: n06-bdp
title: Bandwidth-delay product
spec: Left: a pipe drawn as a rectangle, width labelled bandwidth, length labelled RTT, volume labelled BDP = bandwidth x RTT. Right: table with columns Path, Bandwidth, RTT, BDP: Same rack 100 Gb/s 20 us 250 KB; Same DC 100 Gb/s 100 us 1.25 MB; Metro 10 Gb/s 2 ms 2.5 MB; Cross-continent 10 Gb/s 70 ms 87.5 MB (orange); Intercontinental 10 Gb/s 180 ms 225 MB. Footer: 'a 4 MB window over a 70 ms RTT tops out at about 457 Mb/s on a 10 Gb/s path'. Green bar: 'A window that fills a rack-local path falls far short on a long one'.
cap: The amount of data needed in flight to fill a path grows with bandwidth and distance.

name: n06-loss
title: Two ways TCP notices loss
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Panel 1 'RTO (slow path)': sender sends segment, timer runs, no ACK, retransmit and the RTO doubles (exponential backoff), formula in monospace 'RTO = SRTT + 4 x RTTVAR', minimum 200 ms. Panel 2 'Fast retransmit (cheap)': receiver repeats ACK for last in-order byte (duplicate ACKs), after three duplicate ACKs sender retransmits at once and enters fast recovery (halves its window). Under both a green strip: 'SACK tells the sender exactly what arrived'. Orange note: 'Reordering looks like loss: duplicate ACKs'.
anchor: ## 5. Reliability: ACKs, retransmission and the RTO
cap: A lost segment is detected either by a timer expiring or by three duplicate ACKs.

name: n07-udp
title: UDP header and datagram
spec: Top: UDP header as a 32-bit wide grid, two rows of two fields: Source port | Destination port; Length | Checksum; then 'data ...'. Label 'header is 8 bytes'. Below, three green chips of what UDP lacks, drawn crossed out in orange: 'connection', 'ordering', 'retransmission', 'flow or congestion control'. Bottom note: 'recvfrom returns exactly one datagram; each arrives whole or not at all'. Second note: 'above the path MTU the datagram is fragmented at IP, one lost fragment loses the whole datagram'.
cap: UDP is an 8-byte header with no connection, ordering or retransmission.

name: n07-icmptypes
title: ICMP types you must not block
spec: Two small tables. IPv4: 0 Echo reply (ping response); 3 Destination unreachable (code 3 port, code 4 fragmentation needed and DF set); 5 Redirect; 8 Echo request; 11 Time exceeded (TTL expired, traceroute); 12 Parameter problem. ICMPv6: 1 Destination unreachable; 2 Packet Too Big; 3 Time exceeded; 128/129 Echo request/reply; 133 to 137 neighbour discovery. Orange highlight on 'type 3 code 4' and 'type 2 Packet Too Big' with note 'Path MTU Discovery depends on these'. Green bar: 'Before you block any ICMP type, check which of the types above it would break'.
anchor: ## 2. ICMP: the network layer's error and diagnostic channel
cap: Some ICMP messages such as fragmentation needed and Packet Too Big are required for the network to work.

name: n07-blackhole
title: The PMTU black hole
spec: Timeline between client and server. Green: 'TCP handshake succeeds (tiny packets)'. Green: 'small requests work'. Orange: 'large transfer stalls: big packet dropped, ICMP error blocked, sender never learns the limit'. Right panel step-down test in monospace: 'ping -M do -s 1472 host' then step down 1472, 1452, 1432, 1400 until one passes; also 'tracepath -n host', 'tcpdump -ni any icmp[icmptype]==3 and icmp[icmpcode]==4', 'sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing'. Footer: seen in VPNs, GRE, IPsec, WireGuard, VXLAN, Geneve, GCP default VPC MTU 1460.
cap: With the ICMP error blocked, the handshake and small requests work but large transfers hang.

name: n07-checklist
title: Layered reachability checklist
spec: Numbered ladder of eight steps from bottom to top, each with its command in monospace: 1 interface and address 'ip -br addr'; 2 gateway and neighbour 'ping <gateway>', 'ip neigh'; 3 route 'ip route get <B>'; 4 ICMP 'ping -c3 B', 'traceroute -n B' or 'mtr'; 5 port 'nc -zv B 443'; 6 large packets 'ping -M do -s 1472 B', 'tracepath B'; 7 application 'curl -v'; 8 other end 'tcpdump' on B. Orange highlight on step 5 with note 'refused (RST) and timeout (drop) point to different places'.
cap: Test one layer at a time from the interface up to the application, then look at the far end.

name: n08-records
title: DNS record types
spec: Table with three columns Type, Question it answers, Example (monospace). Rows: A IPv4 address 'gpu01 IN A 10.20.0.45'; AAAA IPv6 address 'gpu01 IN AAAA 2001:db8::45'; CNAME alias 'www IN CNAME lb.example.com.'; NS name servers 'example.com. IN NS ns1.example.com.'; MX mail exchanger 'IN MX 10 mail.example.com.'; PTR reverse mapping '45.0.20.10.in-addr.arpa. IN PTR gpu01.example.com.'; SRV service location '_etcd-server-ssl._tcp IN SRV 0 5 2380 etcd1'; CAA which CAs may issue 'IN CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"'. Orange note on CNAME: 'not allowed at the zone apex'.
cap: Each record type answers a different question about a name.

name: n08-ndots
title: ndots and search domain expansion
spec: Left: a pod's resolv.conf in monospace: 'search my-ns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local dc1.example.com', 'nameserver 10.96.0.10', 'options ndots:5'. Right: a lookup of api.example.com (2 dots, fewer than 5) producing a vertical list of tried names in order: api.example.com.my-ns.svc.cluster.local, then ...svc.cluster.local, then ...cluster.local, then ...dc1.example.com, finally the name itself (orange for the failing wasted ones). Bottom fixes row: 'FQDN with trailing dot', 'dnsConfig.options ndots: 1 or 2', 'NodeLocal DNSCache'.
alt: ndots search expansion in a pod
cap: A name with fewer dots than ndots is tried through every search domain before the real name.

name: n08-5sec
title: The random 5-second delay
spec: Sequence between pod and CoreDNS via node conntrack: pod sends two UDP queries, A and AAAA, from the same source port within microseconds; the AAAA query is lost in conntrack (orange X, race on same-5-tuple UDP flows through NAT); resolver waits 5 s (glibc timeout) then retries and the call stalls. Side fixes in monospace: 'single-request-reopen', 'use-vc', NodeLocal DNSCache, kernel upgrade. Green bar: 'Match the number of seconds to a timer and you will find the layer'.
anchor: ## 11. Case study: "random 5-second delays" in a GPU inference cluster
cap: Two parallel UDP queries can race in conntrack, so one is lost and the resolver waits for its 5 second timeout.

name: n09-relay
title: DHCP relay agent
spec: Left to right: Client in a rack VLAN, a router/switch box labelled 'DHCP relay agent', a central DHCP server. Arrow 1 client to relay: 'DHCP broadcast (does not cross routers)'. Arrow 2 relay to server: 'unicast, relay adds its interface address in giaddr'. Arrow 3 server to client path back: 'server reads giaddr to pick the scope (subnet pool)'. Orange highlight on giaddr. Small options chip: 'option 3 router, 6 DNS, 51 lease time, 66/67 TFTP server and boot file (PXE)'. Monospace for giaddr and option numbers.
cap: A relay agent turns a local broadcast into a unicast to a central server and tags it with giaddr so the server picks the right scope.

name: n09-pxe
title: PXE boot of a bare-metal GPU node
spec: Four numbered steps left to right with arrows. 1 'NIC firmware (PXE ROM or UEFI HTTP boot): DHCP DISCOVER, vendor class PXEClient, option 93 architecture'. 2 'DHCP server replies: address + next-server (TFTP) + filename (for example ipxe.efi)'. 3 'firmware downloads bootloader iPXE; script over HTTP fetches kernel, initrd, kickstart/autoinstall/cloud-init seed'. 4 'OS installer or provisioner (BCM, MAAS, Ironic) configures the node; then node's own DHCP client runs'. Orange note under step 1-2: 'Only one DHCP server may answer a subnet'. Monospace for PXEClient, ipxe.efi.
anchor: ### PXE boot of bare-metal GPU nodes
cap: A bare-metal node gets its address, bootloader, kernel and installer one step at a time over DHCP, TFTP and HTTP.

name: n09-snatdnat
title: SNAT versus DNAT
spec: Two horizontal flows. Top row 'SNAT / PAT (outbound)': private host -> NAT box -> Internet; the NAT box rewrites the SOURCE address (and translated source port for PAT); use: egress to the Internet, MASQUERADE, Cloud NAT. Bottom row 'DNAT (inbound)': client from Internet -> NAT box -> inside server; the NAT box rewrites the DESTINATION; use: port forwarding, Kubernetes Services, Docker -p. Small chip for static NAT (1:1) fixed inside address to fixed outside address, elastic IPs. Orange highlight on 'NAT is not a firewall'. Green bar: 'If you see MASQUERADE in a rule, you are looking at PAT'.
cap: SNAT rewrites the source on the way out and DNAT rewrites the destination on the way in.

name: n10-httpmsg
title: Anatomy of an HTTP exchange
spec: Two stacked boxes, request on top (client to server) and response below, in monospace. Request: 'GET /v1/models HTTP/1.1' (first line: method + target), headers 'Host: api.example.com', 'Accept: application/json', 'Authorization: Bearer eyJ...'. Response: 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' (first line: status), headers 'Content-Type: application/json', 'Content-Length: 142', 'Cache-Control: max-age=60'. Orange highlight on both first lines with note 'read the first line first'. Right side chips for status classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error; note 'A 502, 503 or 504 from a load balancer points to the upstream'.
cap: The first line of each message holds the method and target or the status, and the status class tells you where to look.

name: n10-httpver
title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
spec: Three columns. HTTP/1.1: persistent connections (keep-alive), Host header, over TCP; one connection per request in HTTP/1.0. HTTP/2 (RFC 9113): many streams multiplexed over one TCP connection, binary frames, HPACK header compression, flow control per stream. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114): runs on QUIC over UDP, independent streams so a lost packet on one stream does not block others, faster handshakes, connections can migrate, TLS 1.3 built in. Below each column a small drawing: 1.1 several roads, 2 one road with many lanes, 3 many lanes over UDP. Orange note: 'Reuse connections: saves the TCP and TLS handshake costs, 1 RTT + 1 RTT'.
cap: HTTP/2 shares one TCP connection between streams, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP so streams are independent.

name: n10-crypto
title: What each crypto building block does
spec: Six rows each with a job and examples: Symmetric encryption: fast bulk confidentiality, AES-128/256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305. Key exchange: agree a shared secret over an insecure channel, (EC)DHE X25519, P-256. Public-key signatures: prove possession of a private key, RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519. Hashes: fixed-size fingerprint, SHA-256, SHA-384. HMAC: authenticate with a shared key, HMAC-SHA256. Key derivation: secrets into session keys, HKDF. Green bar: 'No single tool does everything; TLS combines them'. Orange note on Key exchange: 'ephemeral keys give forward secrecy'.
anchor: ## 2. Security goals and cryptographic building blocks
cap: TLS combines symmetric encryption, key exchange, signatures, hashes, HMAC and key derivation, each covering a different job.

name: n10-rtt
title: Round trips: TCP plus TLS
spec: Two horizontal bars comparing connection setup cost before the first request. Top bar 'TCP + TLS 1.2': three blocks 'TCP 1 RTT' + 'TLS 2 RTT' = 3 RTTs. Bottom bar 'TCP + TLS 1.3': blocks 'TCP 1 RTT' + 'TLS 1 RTT' = 2 RTTs (green, shorter). Orange arrow showing the saved round trip. Side note: 'TLS 1.3 client sends its key share in the first message'. Footer: 'Session tickets or PSKs let a returning client skip the full handshake'.
cap: TCP plus TLS 1.3 takes 2 round trips instead of 3 for TLS 1.2.

name: n11-cutthrough
title: Store-and-forward versus cut-through
spec: Two timelines of one frame through a switch. Top 'Store-and-forward': receive the whole frame, verify FCS, then forward; latency grows with frame size (9000-byte jumbo on 10 Gb/s needs 7.2 us to serialise). Bottom 'Cut-through': starts forwarding as soon as the destination header is read; latency roughly constant, hundreds of nanoseconds; cost: corrupt frames may get through, the last hop's FCS check drops them (orange). Footer formula in monospace: 'Serialization delay = frame bits / link rate'. Note: port-to-port latency typically 300 ns to 1 us.
cap: Store-and-forward checks the whole frame first, while cut-through starts sending after the destination header.

name: n11-portmodes
title: Access, trunk and native VLAN ports
spec: A switch in the middle. Left: three hosts on access ports labelled 'Access: one VLAN, frames leave untagged'. Right: trunk link to a second switch labelled 'Trunk: multiple VLANs with 802.1Q tags (allowed list)', with one VLAN on it shown untagged and labelled 'Native (untagged) VLAN'. Orange warning: 'Mismatched native VLANs leak traffic across VLANs and trigger STP warnings'. Bottom practices strip: 'do not use VLAN 1', 'prune trunks', 'black-hole VLAN for unused ports'.
cap: Access ports carry one untagged VLAN, trunks carry many tagged VLANs, and the native VLAN is the one sent untagged.

name: n11-intervlan
title: Inter-VLAN routing
spec: Panel A 'Router-on-a-stick': one trunk from a switch to a router with sub-interfaces eth0.10 and eth0.20, each holding the gateway IP of its VLAN. Panel B 'SVI / IRB': an interface per VLAN on an L3 switch. Panel C 'Data centre': VLAN gateway moves to the leaf switch; VLANs rarely extend beyond a rack or pair of leaves; stretch with EVPN/VXLAN (chapter 2.17). Monospace for sub-interface names. Orange note: 'A VLAN is a closed broadcast domain, so different VLANs need an L3 gateway'.
cap: Hosts in different VLANs reach each other only through a layer 3 gateway, built as sub-interfaces, SVIs or on the leaf.

name: n12-lacp
title: LACP modes and timers
spec: Left: a 3x3 matrix of the two ends' modes. Rows end A, columns end B: active/active bundle forms quickly (green); active/passive bundle forms, active speaks first (green); passive/passive nothing negotiates, each waits for the other (orange). Right: two timer cards: slow = hello every 30 s, timeout after 90 s; fast = hello every 1 s, timeout after 3 s. Note: 'static on mode creates a bundle without LACP'. Footer: frames flow only on members in the 'collecting/distributing' state.
cap: At least one end must be active for LACP to form a bundle, and fast timers detect failures in 3 seconds.

name: n12-bondmodes
title: Linux bonding modes
spec: Table with columns Mode, Name (monospace), Behaviour, Switch support: 0 balance-rr per-packet round robin, static bundle, reordering risk; 1 active-backup one active member, none needed (orange as practical choice 1); 2 balance-xor hash of MAC or xmit_hash_policy, static bundle; 3 broadcast all members, rare; 4 802.3ad LACP (orange, practical choice 2), LACP on the switch; 5 balance-tlb none; 6 balance-alb none. Footer green bar: 'For servers two modes are practical: active-backup and LACP'.
cap: Mode 1 active-backup and mode 4 LACP are the two practical choices for servers.

name: n12-resilient
title: Modulo versus resilient hashing
spec: Two panels with four path boxes each. Left 'Plain hash mod N': one path fails, N changes, 75% of all flows move to a different path (orange), even though only a quarter were on the failed path. Right 'Resilient hashing': only the 25% on the failed path move, the three healthy paths keep every flow (green). Footer: 'nothing on healthy paths is reordered or reset'. Side note: ECMP paths need not connect the same two devices.
cap: Resilient hashing moves only the flows from the failed path instead of reshuffling almost all flows.

name: n13-dijkstra
title: Dijkstra on a small diamond
spec: A diamond graph: root A at top, B and C in the middle, D at the bottom; links A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D each labelled cost 10. Step labels beside it: 1 'root A in the tree at cost 0, all others infinity'; 2 'closest nodes B and C join the tree at cost 10'; 3 'relax neighbours: D is reached through both B and C'; 4 'install the lowest-cost next hops, including every equal-cost one for ECMP' (orange on the two equal paths to D). Green bar: 'Every router computes from an identical database, so the results are loop-free'.
cap: Each router runs Dijkstra on the same database and keeps every equal-cost next hop.

name: n13-families
title: Three routing families compared
spec: Table with three columns Distance vector, Link state, Path vector and rows: Knows (distances and next hops / whole topology / paths, AS lists); State per router (low / high LSDB / per-prefix per-path); Loop avoidance (split horizon or DUAL / consistent database and SPF / own ID in path); Convergence (slower RIP, fast DUAL / fast / slow without tuning); Policy (limited / limited / rich); Examples (RIP, EIGRP / OSPF, IS-IS / BGP). Orange highlight on the Convergence row for path vector. Header chips in green.
alt: Distance vector, link state and path vector
cap: Each routing family trades state, convergence speed and policy richness differently.

name: n13-redistloop
title: Redistribution loop and the tag fix
spec: Two panels. Left 'Loop': routers A and B between protocol X and protocol Y clouds; A injects prefix N from X into Y; B hears N from Y and injects it back into X; arrow loops with orange label 'N now looks like a new route'. Right 'Tag fix': OSPF into BGP with 'set tag 1001' on the way in, and 'route-map BGP-TO-OSPF deny 5, match tag 1001' blocking the way back (green). Footer chips: 'keep redistribution one way', 'send defaults down and aggregates up', 'route tags'. Monospace for route-map lines.
cap: A route injected from one protocol into another can come back, and a route tag marks it so it is blocked on the way back.

name: n14-drbdr
title: Why OSPF elects a DR and BDR
spec: Two panels with routers drawn as dots on one Ethernet segment. Left 'Full mesh': 4 routers with all 6 pairwise adjacency lines; caption '4 routers need 6 relationships, 10 routers need 45; n(n-1)/2'. Right 'DR and BDR': same 4 routers, one marked DR and one BDR (orange), other two connected only to the DR and BDR: each other router keeps just two. Footer: 'Election: highest priority, then highest router ID. Data-centre fabrics use ip ospf network point-to-point (no election)'. Monospace for the command.
cap: Electing a DR and BDR cuts the number of adjacencies on a shared segment from n(n-1)/2 to two per router.

name: n14-cost
title: OSPF cost and reference bandwidth
spec: Formula in monospace at top: 'cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth (minimum 1)'. Two rows. Row 'Default reference 100 Mb/s': 1G link cost 1, 100G link cost 1 (orange, both look identical, SPF cannot tell them apart). Row 'Reference raised to 400000 Mb/s': the two links get clearly different costs and SPF prefers the fast one (green). Side note: 'timers throttle spf 50 100 5000' = initial delay, hold time, maximum.
cap: With the default 100 Mb/s reference, a 1G and a 100G link have the same cost of 1.

name: n14-net
title: IS-IS NET address anatomy
spec: A single address strip in monospace '49.0001 . 1921.6800.1001 . 00' split into three labelled segments: '49.0001 = AFI + area (49 is the private AFI, 0001 is the area)', '1921.6800.1001 = System ID (6 bytes, unique within the domain)', '00 = N-selector (always 00 for a router)'. Below, three chips: 'Level 1: knows its own area', 'Level 2: backbone between areas', 'L1/L2: connects both (default)'. Orange note: 'Same area address means same area and flooding domain; mismatched areas form only Level 2 adjacencies'. Green bar: 'For a single-area data-centre underlay run everything as Level 2 only'.
cap: A NET has an area part, a unique System ID and an N-selector of 00.

name: n14-choose
title: OSPF or IS-IS
spec: Comparison table, columns Consideration, Prefer OSPF, Prefer IS-IS. Rows: Familiarity (everywhere / strong in carriers, less in enterprise); IPv4+IPv6 (v2+v3 or AFs / one process carries both); Hierarchy (areas with ABRs / levels, boundary on links); Extensibility (LSA types / TLVs, easy); Adjacency independence from IP (needs IP / doesn't); MPLS TE and SR (supported / strong heritage). Green bar: 'Choose the one your organisation can operate'.
cap: Both converge in sub-second time with tuning and BFD, so pick the one your team can operate.

name: n15-attrs
title: BGP path attribute categories
spec: Four stacked rows with a category, meaning and examples: Well-known mandatory (must be understood and present in every UPDATE): ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP; Well-known discretionary (understood, may be omitted): LOCAL_PREF, ATOMIC_AGGREGATE; Optional transitive (passed along if unknown): COMMUNITY, AGGREGATOR, Large Community; Optional non-transitive (dropped if not understood): MED, ORIGINATOR_ID, CLUSTER_LIST. Right side note chips: 'LOCAL_PREF: higher wins, default 100, travels only inside an AS'; 'MED: lower wins'. Monospace for attribute names.
cap: Attribute categories decide what each router must understand and what it passes on.

name: n15-aspath
title: AS_PATH loop prevention
spec: Small triangle-plus-one topology: A (AS65000) advertises 2001:db8:100::/64 to B and C. B (AS65001) re-advertises it to D with path [65001, 65000]. D is AS65003. Each AS box shows the path stack it carries, with each hop prepending its own ASN. Orange note on a looped path: 'a router rejects any route that already contains its own ASN'. Top note: 'BGP has no split horizon; loops are still prevented'. Monospace for prefix and path lists.
cap: Each AS prepends its number, and any router rejects a route that already carries its own.

name: n15-ebgpibgp
title: eBGP versus iBGP
spec: Two columns. eBGP: peers in different ASes, normally directly connected; next hop rewritten to the sender's address; local AS prepended to AS_PATH; TTL 1 by default. iBGP: peers in the same AS, usually loopback to loopback and multihop over the IGP; AS_PATH not modified; next hop not changed by default, so the IGP must reach the original eBGP next hop. Orange bottom note: 'Choose the session type first: the session comes up fine either way'.
cap: The session type decides the next hop, the AS_PATH and the TTL you must plan for.

name: n15-rr
title: Full mesh versus route reflector
spec: Two panels. Left 'iBGP full mesh': routers in a ring with all pairs connected; text '100 routers need 4,950 iBGP sessions'. Right 'Route reflector': one RR in the centre with client routers connected only to it; text 'two route reflectors serving the same hundred routers: 197 sessions' (green). Caveat strip in orange: 'RR picks best paths from its own IGP-cost view, which can hide path diversity'. Monospace commands row: 'neighbor X next-hop-self', 'update-source lo'.
anchor: ## 5. Advertisement rules, iBGP scaling and route reflectors
cap: A route reflector replaces thousands of iBGP sessions with a handful.

name: n16-valley
title: Why all spines share one ASN
spec: Leaf-spine slice with leaf3, spine1, spine2, leaf2 (spine1 and spine2 same ASN, shown in the same colour). Path arrows: route starts at leaf3, goes up to spine1, down to leaf2 where a failed link (orange X) leaves only one remaining path, then leaf2 passes the route up to spine2: spine2 sees its own ASN already in the path and rejects it (green check on the rejection). Second small panel 'different spine ASNs: no repeated ASN, the valley path is installed, forwarding becomes suboptimal and latency rises' in orange. Note: per-rack leaf ASN 65101, 65102.
cap: Giving all spines one ASN makes eBGP loop prevention reject valley paths after multiple failures.

name: n16-unnumbered
title: BGP unnumbered step by step
spec: Two switches cabled together, no IP typed on either end. Numbered steps: 1 'each interface gets an automatic link-local address fe80::/64'; 2 'each side sends IPv6 Router Advertisements and Neighbour Discovery; FRR learns the neighbour link-local address and MAC'; 3 'TCP session starts to port 179'; 4 'OPEN carries Extended Next Hop Encoding capability (RFC 8950), so IPv4 routes work on a link with no IPv4 address'. Config chip in monospace: 'neighbor swp1 interface remote-as external'. Orange side stat: '32 leaves x 16 spines = 512 links to address by hand'.
cap: Link-local IPv6 addresses and the extended next hop capability remove the need for a subnet on every link.

name: n16-blackhole
title: The Clos black-hole caveat
spec: Fabric drawing: border at the top, four spines, leaf3 at the bottom. Every spine advertises aggregate 10.10.0.0/16. A broken link (orange X) between leaf3 and spine2. The border sees one covering route from all spines and sprays the client's flows across all four, including spine2, which still advertises the aggregate but cannot reach leaf3, so those packets are dropped (orange). Rules strip: 'do not summarise where a specific route is needed for correctness', 'summarise only toward the outside, at the border or WAN'.
cap: An aggregate advertised by a spine that has lost its path keeps attracting traffic it cannot deliver.

name: n16-addpath
title: ADD-PATH
spec: Two panels. Left 'Default': two border leaves announce the same destination to a spine; the spine's best-path rule picks one winner and tells the leaf only about that one; the second path sits idle (orange). Right 'ADD-PATH': the spine advertises every working path to the leaf, so the leaf can use both (green). Side analogy chip: 'dispatch board lists only the fastest route'.
cap: ADD-PATH lets a speaker advertise all good paths instead of only its single best path.

name: n16-ucmp
title: Weighted ECMP with link bandwidth
spec: Two panels. Left 'Plain ECMP': one leaf with four next-hop links of different capacity, each receiving an equal quarter of the traffic (orange on the narrow link). Right 'Link Bandwidth Extended Community': advertising router encodes link speed in the community; the receiver assigns weights proportional to capacity (weighted ECMP, also called UCMP) (green). Footer: 'if a spine loses a link to the super-spine, it advertises reduced capacity and leaves send proportionally less through it'.
anchor: ### Link Bandwidth Extended Community and weighted ECMP
cap: The link bandwidth community lets receivers split traffic in proportion to each path's capacity.

name: n17-encapoverhead
title: Encapsulation overhead and ECMP entropy
spec: Horizontal bar chart of overhead in bytes (IPv4 underlay), one bar per encapsulation: GRE 24 B; IPIP 20 B; VXLAN 50 B (outer Ethernet 14 + IP 20 + UDP 8 + VXLAN 8); GENEVE 50+ B; MPLS 4 B per label; WireGuard 60 B; IPsec ESP about 50 to 73 B. Each bar tagged 'UDP-based: ECMP entropy from outer source port' (VXLAN, GENEVE, WireGuard, green) or 'no ports: all traffic between two endpoints hashes to one path' (GRE, IPIP, ESP, orange). Footer: 'VXLAN is L2 over UDP/4789, GENEVE UDP/6081'.
cap: Each tunnel type adds a different number of header bytes, and only UDP-based ones give ECMP something to hash.

name: n17-evpnlayers
title: EVPN: underlay and overlay
spec: Two stacked layers. Bottom 'Underlay': eBGP, OSPF or IS-IS ECMP fabric giving IP reachability between VTEP loopbacks; spines and leaves drawn. Top 'Overlay': EVPN as an extra BGP address family on the leaf-spine sessions; spines act as route servers, not tunnel endpoints; leaves are VTEPs with VXLAN tunnels between them. A callout: 'BGP tells every VTEP where each MAC and IP lives, so no flooding to learn'. Small chips: EVI = MAC-VRF for an L2 segment; IP-VRF for L3 routing; RD makes routes unique across VRFs.
anchor: ## 4. EVPN: a control plane for Ethernet and IP overlays
cap: The underlay gives VTEPs IP reachability, and EVPN over BGP tells each VTEP where hosts live.

name: n17-evpnroutes
title: The five EVPN route types
spec: Five numbered rows with type, name and purpose: 1 Ethernet Auto-Discovery: multihoming, fast convergence and aliasing; 2 MAC/IP Advertisement: host MAC (and optionally IP) with VNI and VTEP next hop, MAC mobility (orange, heart of host reachability); 3 Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag: builds the BUM replication list, 'I am in VNI x'; 4 Ethernet Segment: designated-forwarder election among multihomed leaves; 5 IP Prefix: prefixes into IP-VRFs. Bracket on types 1 and 4: 'multihoming'.
cap: Type 2 carries host reachability, while types 1 and 4 handle multihoming, 3 builds the BUM list and 5 carries prefixes.

name: n17-evpnpitfalls
title: Common EVPN and VXLAN pitfalls
spec: Checklist card with ten items, each with a small warning icon: underlay MTU too small; VTEP loopbacks not advertised; route targets mismatched (routes arrive, never imported); duplicate anycast gateway MAC on two leaves; a spine rewrites next hops; asymmetric IRB forces every leaf to carry every VNI; ARP suppression disabled (BUM storms); ECMP polarization when the hash ignores the outer UDP source port; missing resilient hashing or MLAG mixed with EVPN multihoming; default import of any lets tenant routes leak. Orange highlight on the first item. Green bar: 'Before you turn on EVPN, check route targets match and the underlay MTU is large enough'.
cap: Most EVPN faults come from a short list of MTU, advertisement, route target and hashing mistakes.

name: n18-sizing
title: Sizing a 3-stage fabric
spec: Left: formulas for R-port switches at 1:1: 'spines = R/2', 'max leaves = R', 'max servers = R x R/2 = R^2/2'. Right: worked example with 64-port 400G switches: each leaf 32 downlinks + 32 uplinks, 32 spines, up to 64 leaves, up to 2,048 endpoint ports = 256 servers with eight GPUs each. Small leaf-spine drawing with a leaf split into 'half down to servers / half up to spines'. Orange note: 'beyond R^2/2 endpoints, build pods: 5-stage reaches R^3/4 (65,536 for R = 64)'.
cap: With R-port switches a 1:1 three-stage fabric reaches R squared over two endpoints.

name: n18-fivestage
title: Scaling table: 3-stage to 5-stage
spec: Table with columns Config, GPUs, Leaves, Spines, Super-spines, Oversubscription. Rows: 1 row (one rail group) 256 / 8 / 4 / none / 1:1; 2 rows 512 / 16 / 8 / none / 1:1; 8 rows (3-stage, 64-port) 2,048 / 64 / 32 / none / 1:1; 5-stage 1K-GPU blocks 2,048 / 64 / 64 / 32 / 1:1; 5-stage 4 blocks 4,096 / 128 / 128 / 32 / 2:1 at super-spine; 5-stage 8 blocks 8,192 / 256 / 256 / 32 / 4:1 at super-spine (orange). Divider line between the 3-stage rows and 5-stage rows labelled 'add pods and super-spines'.
cap: Growing beyond one three-stage build needs super-spines or oversubscription of the upper tier.

name: n18-oversub
title: Oversubscription ratios
spec: Leaf switch drawn with server-facing ports below and uplinks above, two worked cases. Case 1: d downlinks and u uplinks gives ratio d:u; 48 downlinks and 16 uplinks = 3:1. Case 2: ToR with 320 Gb/s of server ports and 180 Gb/s of uplinks = 1.78:1. Definition line: 'oversubscription = bandwidth offered to endpoints over bandwidth into the fabric (worst-case contention)'. Orange note: 'Non-blocking and non-contending are different; packet-switched fabrics cannot be truly non-blocking because of incast'.
cap: Oversubscription is the ratio of server bandwidth to uplink bandwidth at a tier.

name: n18-failure
title: Capacity left after a spine fails
spec: Bar comparison. Formula in monospace: 'capacity kept = (S-1)/S of uplink capacity'. Two bars: S = 32 spines, one down: 96.9% (green, almost full); S = 4 spines, one down: 75% (orange). Small leaf with its uplinks, one greyed out. Footer: 'A 1:1 design stays oversubscribed until the failure is repaired' and bar 'Work out what survives losing one spine, one leaf and one rail group'.
cap: The fewer spines a fabric has, the bigger the capacity loss when one spine fails.

name: n19-markings
title: Where QoS markings live
spec: Stack of header strips each showing its QoS field: IPv4/IPv6 header: ToS or Traffic Class byte = DSCP (6 bits, 64 values: CS0..CS7, AF11..AF43, EF=46, DF=0) + ECN (2 bits); Ethernet 802.1Q tag: PCP (3 bits, 0 to 7) + DEI; MPLS: traffic class (3 bits); Layer 4: ports, RoCEv2 on UDP 4791. Right side example plan in orange: 'RoCE data class DSCP 26 mapped to priority 3', 'CNP class DSCP 48 to strict-priority or high-weight queue'. Footer: 're-mark untrusted markings at the edge'. Monospace for DSCP values.
cap: DSCP, PCP and MPLS traffic class each carry the class a packet belongs to at a different layer.

name: n19-policeshape
title: Policer versus shaper
spec: Two panels with the same bursty traffic curve crossing a rate line. Left 'Policer (the bouncer)': traffic above the committed rate is dropped or remarked; token bucket measures CIR and burst size. Right 'Shaper (the queue marshal)': excess is buffered and released at the configured rate; smooths bursts but adds delay and needs buffer space. Footer: 'The burst size, the bucket depth, matters as much as the rate: a deep bucket lets a short burst through, a shallow one clips it'.
cap: A policer drops or remarks excess traffic, while a shaper buffers it and releases it at the configured rate.

name: n19-congestionpoints
title: Where congestion appears in a fabric
spec: Small leaf-spine-super-spine drawing with numbered markers: 1 Leaf downlink (leaf to server): incast; 2 Local leaf switching: two servers sending to a third on the same leaf; 3 Leaf to spine uplink: hash collisions put elephant flows on one uplink; 4 Spine to leaf downlink: flows from several leaves converge on one link; 5 Spine to super-spine: same effects plus oversubscription; 6 Microbursts: sub-millisecond bursts invisible to average counters (orange). Footer: 'Find out which point is actually congested before tuning load balancing'.
alt: Congestion points in a Clos fabric
cap: Congestion can appear at every tier of a 1:1 fabric, from the leaf downlink to microbursts.

name: n19-dcqcn
title: DCQCN threshold ladder
spec: A vertical queue-depth axis in KB with markers bottom to top: XON 50 KB; Kmin 100 KB (ECN marking starts); Kmax 500 KB with Pmax 0.20 (marking probability tops out); XOFF 1000 KB (PFC pause). Left bracket 'ECN: early, flow-level signal, egress queue thresholds: switch marks, receiver sends CNP, sender reduces rate' (green). Upper bracket 'PFC: last-resort safety net, ingress buffer thresholds' (orange). Footer: 'ECN acts first and PFC is the backstop; XON sits below XOFF'.
cap: ECN marking starts well below the PFC XOFF level so senders slow down before any pause.

name: n20-families
title: Load balancing families by layer
spec: Ladder of six rows from coarse to fine, each with the decision it makes and examples: DNS / GSLB: name resolution (Route 53, Cloud DNS routing policies); L3 ECMP / anycast: flow hash across equal-cost next hops (router ECMP, BGP-announced VIPs); L4: TCP/UDP connections, 5-tuple (IPVS/LVS, Maglev, Katran, HAProxy mode tcp); L7: HTTP/gRPC requests, headers, paths (HAProxy mode http, nginx, Envoy, ALB); Client-side: gRPC round_robin with xDS; In-cluster / mesh: kube-proxy, Cilium eBPF, Envoy sidecar. Arrow on the side: 'Lower layers decide faster but see less'. Orange on L4 row: 'cannot see requests inside a connection'.
cap: Lower-layer balancers decide faster but see less of each request.

name: n20-anycast
title: Scaling the L4 tier with ECMP and anycast
spec: Four numbered steps around one VIP. Step 1: each L4 node announces the VIP over BGP (FRR, BIRD or ExaBGP); the router sees N equal-cost next hops and spreads flows by 5-tuple hash. Step 2: a node fails or drains, BGP session drops (BFD under a second), router removes it, its flows are remapped. Step 3: surviving nodes get flows they hold no state for, so L4 balancers use Maglev-style consistent hashing on the 5-tuple. Step 4: L4 node forwards to backend by DSR, encapsulation, or proxying. Orange note under step 2: 'plain modulo hashing may rehash all flows'. Footer: 'Decide your failover budget first: BGP convergence sets how fast traffic moves'.
anchor: ## 4. ECMP, anycast and scaling out the L4 tier
cap: Many L4 nodes announce the same VIP and the router spreads flows across them, with consistent hashing keeping connections intact.

name: n20-tlsplace
title: Where TLS ends
spec: Client on the left, load balancer in the middle, backends on the right, two rows. Row 1 'TLS termination at the LB': LB decrypts, can inspect and route at L7 (headers, WAF), then re-encrypts or sends plaintext to the backends. Row 2 'Passthrough': an L4 balancer routes on SNI and keeps the traffic encrypted. Below: client IP preservation chips: 'L7: X-Forwarded-For or Forwarded (trust only from known proxies)', 'L4: PROXY protocol v1 or v2', 'DSR and externalTrafficPolicy: Local avoid SNAT'. Green bar: 'Decide where TLS ends before anything else: it sets what the balancer can route on'.
anchor: ## 7. TLS, client identity and L4/L7 interplay
cap: Where TLS ends decides what the balancer can read and route on.

name: n20-pinning
title: Connection pinning with gRPC
spec: Two panels with clients on the left and five backends on the right. Left 'L4 rule in front of gRPC port (per connection)': every client opened one long connection, so all its streams go to one backend; servers 1 and 2 are overloaded (orange) while 3 to 5 sit idle. Right 'L7 proxy or client-side balancing (per request)': requests spread evenly (green). Footer: 'Balance per request, not per connection; avoid pure L4 for multiplexed gRPC'. Monospace for grpc_pass.
cap: An L4 balancer pins each long gRPC connection to one backend, so per-request balancing is needed.

name: n21-dos
title: Four kinds of denial of service
spec: Four-row table with columns Type, Mechanism, Mitigation. Volumetric: saturate bandwidth (UDP floods, DNS/NTP/memcached reflection) -> upstream scrubbing or anycast, BCP38, RTBH. Protocol/state exhaustion: SYN floods, connection table exhaustion, fragment attacks -> SYN cookies, connection limits, bigger tables, proxies. Application layer: HTTP floods, slow-loris, expensive queries -> rate limiting, WAF, caching, request cost limits. Control-plane: flood router CPUs with ICMP/ARP/routing packets -> CoPP, ICMP rate limiting, routing protocol authentication. Orange highlight on the line 'Inference APIs: one expensive prompt costs GPU seconds'. Green bar: 'Set your rate limits and quotas before traffic spikes, not during an attack'.
cap: Each kind of denial of service exhausts a different resource and needs a different defence.

name: n21-l2sec
title: Layer-2 attacks and their controls
spec: Seven pairs, attack on the left, control on the right, joined by arrows: MAC flooding / CAM overflow -> port security (limit MACs per port), storm control; Rogue DHCP server -> DHCP snooping, IP source guard; ARP/ND spoofing -> Dynamic ARP Inspection, RA guard; Rogue switch / STP manipulation -> BPDU guard, root guard; VLAN hopping -> disable DTP, no VLAN 1 native, prune trunks; Unauthorised device attach -> 802.1X (EAP-TLS) or MAB; Link eavesdropping -> MACsec (802.1AE). Orange on DHCP snooping row with note 'trust only uplink and server ports'. Green bar: '802.1X decides which devices may attach; MACsec protects the link itself'.
cap: Each layer 2 attack has a matching switch control.

name: n21-netpol
title: Default deny, then allow the gateway
spec: Kubernetes namespace box labelled 'inference'. Inside: a gateway pod (label app: gateway) and a Triton model server pod (label app: triton), plus another pod. Two policy layers: first 'default-deny: podSelector {} , policyTypes Ingress, Egress' shown as a closed outer wall; second 'allow-gateway-to-triton' shown as one green arrow from gateway to triton labelled 'TCP 8001'. Other arrows to triton are blocked (orange X). Footer: 'Allow DNS egress and metrics scraping when you enforce default-deny egress; a policy does nothing unless the CNI enforces it'. Monospace for labels and port.
cap: A default-deny policy plus one allow rule lets only the gateway reach the Triton pod on TCP 8001.

name: n22-socketlife
title: Life cycle of a TCP server socket
spec: Vertical flow of calls in monospace: 'socket()' -> 'bind(addr:port)' -> 'listen(backlog)' -> loop: 'accept()' returns a NEW connected socket -> 'read/recv' and 'write/send' on it -> 'close'. Side notes: 'Sockets are file descriptors: /proc/<pid>/fd, limited by ulimit -n and fs.file-max'; 'Binding to 0.0.0.0 or :: listens on all addresses; the address you bind decides who can reach the service'. Right chips of socket types: SOCK_STREAM (TCP), SOCK_DGRAM (UDP), SOCK_RAW (ICMP tools), AF_PACKET (tcpdump). Orange highlight on accept() with note 'returns a new socket'.
anchor: ## 4. Sockets: how processes use the network
cap: A server calls socket, bind and listen, then accept returns a new connected socket for each client.

name: n22-ssti
title: Reading ss -ti output
spec: The ss -ti example block in monospace in the centre: 'ESTAB 0 0 10.0.0.2:51234 10.0.0.5:443', 'cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.31/0.12 mss:1448 pmtu:1500 cwnd:10 ssthresh:7 bytes_sent:2.1M bytes_acked:2.1M', 'bytes_retrans:12K segs_out:1500 segs_in:900 send 373Mbps pacing_rate 746Mbps delivery_rate 330Mbps', 'busy:2300ms rwnd_limited:100ms(4.3%) app_limited retrans:0/9 reordering:3 rcv_space:14480'. Callouts pointing at fields: cubic = congestion control; rtt:avg/var = round-trip time; cwnd and ssthresh = congestion window state; retrans:current/total = retransmits; delivery_rate = what the connection actually achieves, pacing_rate = what it is allowed. Orange highlight on rwnd_limited.
cap: Each ss -ti field describes one aspect of how a single connection is performing.

name: n22-checklist
title: Top-down and bottom-up checklist
spec: Two vertical ladders side by side with a shared 8-rung list. Top-down (application symptom to wire): 1 process listening 'ss -tulpn'; 2 connect test 'nc -zv host port', refusal versus timeout; 3 DNS 'getent hosts', 'dig'; 4 route and source 'ip route get <dst>', 'ip rule', rp_filter; 5 firewall 'nft list ruleset', conntrack; 6 neighbours 'ip neigh', 'arping'; 7 interface 'ip -s link', 'ethtool -S'; 8 capture packets at both ends. Bottom-up goes the other way: link up, speed and FEC, errors, ring buffers, IRQ and CPU. Orange bar: 'Application reports the failure: go top-down. Counters already rising: go bottom-up'.
anchor: ## 8. Putting it together: a top-down and bottom-up checklist
cap: Start at the application when it reports the failure, and at the hardware when counters are already rising.

name: n22-netmanagers
title: Who configures the network
spec: Layered diagram. Top: cloud-init (generates Netplan, NM or networkd config from metadata). Middle: Netplan (YAML in /etc/netplan/*.yaml; netplan try/apply/generate) renders to either of two boxes: NetworkManager (/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/, nmcli) or systemd-networkd (/etc/systemd/network/*.network, networkctl). Side: ifupdown (/etc/network/interfaces) on older Debian; udev .link files pin interface names (net.ifnames=0). Monospace for paths. Orange note: 'Manual ip changes are not persisted: after reboot config lost'.
cap: Netplan and cloud-init are front ends that render configuration for NetworkManager or systemd-networkd.

name: n23-natfirst
title: NAT applies to the first packet only
spec: Timeline of a flow through a Linux NAT gateway. Packet 1 goes through the nat table where the SNAT or DNAT rule matches, and the translation is written into conntrack (green). Packets 2..n skip the nat table: conntrack applies the stored translation automatically in both directions. A side box: 'Edit the NAT rule: existing flows keep the old translation until their entries are deleted or expire' (orange). Notes: 'snat to 203.0.113.9 = static address'; 'masquerade = interface address, flushes entries when the interface goes down'; 'about 64k ports per destination address and port: port exhaustion'. Monospace for rules.
cap: Only the first packet of a flow traverses the nat table, and conntrack applies the stored translation to the rest.

name: n23-states
title: Conntrack states
spec: A small state journey. A new visitor arrives: NEW (first packet of a flow, no reply seen) -> reply comes back -> ESTABLISHED (traffic seen in both directions). Side branches: RELATED (new flow related to an existing one, FTP data connection or ICMP error), INVALID (violates the state machine, out-of-window TCP, unsolicited ACK; usually drop, orange), UNTRACKED (exempted via raw/NOTRACK). Footer green bar: 'With conntrack, a rule that says allow established is enough'. Monospace for state names.
cap: A flow moves from NEW to ESTABLISHED once traffic is seen in both directions.

name: n23-exhaust
title: Conntrack table full
spec: Left: a table box labelled 'conntrack table: nf_conntrack_buckets (hash) and nf_conntrack_max (cap)' filled up; text 'table full: new connections dropped silently; dmesg: nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet; conntrack -S counts insert_failed' (orange). Right: five numbered remedies in order: 1 find who creates the flows (conntrack -L, conntrack -E); 2 shorten timeouts (established default 5 days = 432,000 s, example 3600 s; time_wait 30 s); 3 raise nf_conntrack_max, buckets max/4 to max/8; 4 bypass with notrack in the raw hook; 5 move to an eBPF datapath. Green bar: 'Start with the first remedy, because it addresses the cause'.
cap: A full conntrack table drops new connections silently, and five remedies are applied in order.

name: n24-pbrfix
title: Per-NIC routing table fix
spec: Server with eth0 10.0.0.5/24 (gateway 10.0.0.1, management) and eth1 192.168.1.5/24 (storage, gateway 192.168.1.1). Left problem in orange: request comes in on eth1, reply leaves via the default route out of eth0 with the storage address as its source. Right fix in green: 'ip rule add from 192.168.1.5/32 lookup storage priority 1000' selects table 'storage' (200 storage in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables) which holds 'default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth1' and the connected route. Verification chip in monospace: 'ip route get 10.50.0.9 from 192.168.1.5 iif lo' shows via 192.168.1.1 dev eth1. Footer: 'also rp_filter 2, arp_ignore=1, arp_announce=2'.
cap: A rule that selects a per-NIC table by source address makes replies leave through the NIC they arrived on.

name: n24-vrf
title: VRF on Linux
spec: Two stacked routing-table boxes inside one Linux host. Box 1 'main table' with eth0. Box 2 'vrf-blue (table 10)' with eth2 10.9.0.5/24, drawn as a separate lane. Note: 'two VRFs can both use 10.9.0.0/24 without mixing' (second lane greyed). Commands in monospace: 'ip link add vrf-blue type vrf table 10', 'ip link set eth2 master vrf-blue', 'ip vrf exec vrf-blue ping 10.9.0.1'. Caveats strip in orange: 'services must start inside the VRF or be VRF-aware (tcp_l3mdev_accept, udp_l3mdev_accept, ip vrf exec)'; 'DNS and NTP resolvers must be reachable in the VRF'.
cap: A VRF gives a group of interfaces its own routing table so identical address ranges do not collide.

name: n24-rss
title: Spreading a flow across queues and cores
spec: Left to right: NIC with receive queues Q0 to Q3, each with its own interrupt (IRQ) pointing to a different CPU core (core 0 to 3). A flow's addresses and ports are hashed (Toeplitz) to pick one queue, so each flow stays on one core, keeping packet order and cache. Below: three options in a row: 'RSS: hardware, NIC hashes to N receive queues (ethtool -l eth0)'; 'RPS: software, steers to other CPUs after the interrupt'; 'XPS: maps CPUs to TX queues, avoids lock contention and cross-NUMA transmit'. Orange note: 'One core cannot process 100 Gb/s on its own'. Footer check: 'mpstat -P ALL 1: is one core at 100%?'.
cap: Hardware queues and software steering spread traffic across cores while each flow stays on one core.

name: n24-offloads
title: NIC offloads: which to keep
spec: Table with columns Offload, What it does, Advice. Rows: Checksum offload: NIC computes/validates L4 checksums; capture on sender shows 'bad cksum' (benign). TSO/GSO: send 64 KB buffers, segmented into MTU-sized frames; big CPU saver, enable (green). GRO: merge received packets into larger skbs; may hurt forwarding, bridges, latency; disable on routers and VXLAN gateways (orange). LRO: hardware merge on receive; breaks forwarding, avoid on routers, bridges, hypervisors (orange). Flow control (802.3x pause): usually off in modern DCs, PFC instead. Command row in monospace: 'ethtool -k eth0', 'ethtool -K eth0 tso on gso on gro on lro off'.
cap: TSO and GSO save CPU, but GRO and LRO can break routers and bridges.

name: n25-netns
title: What a network namespace owns
spec: A host box containing two namespace boxes side by side, 'red' and 'default'. Inside each a stack of items: own interfaces, own IP addresses, own routing tables, own ARP and ND neighbour tables, own netfilter rules, own conntrack table, own /proc/net. Callout: 'two containers can both serve on port 8080: each has its own port space'. Monospace commands under 'red': 'ip netns add red', 'ip netns exec red ip link' (only a down loopback at first), 'ip -n red link set lo up'. Orange note: 'nsenter -t <pid> -n ip addr enters a container namespace by PID'.
cap: A network namespace is a complete independent copy of the network stack, so each container has its own ports, routes and firewall.

name: n25-dockermodes
title: Docker network modes
spec: Table with columns Mode, Behaviour, Use. bridge (default docker0): private subnet, veth per container, NAT outbound, -p publishes via DNAT. host (--network host): shares the host namespace, no isolation, no NAT, best performance, ports conflict (use: NCCL/HPC containers). none: only loopback. container:NAME: shares another container's namespace (sidecars; how a Kubernetes pod works). overlay: VXLAN across Docker hosts (Swarm). macvlan / ipvlan: container on the physical network. Orange highlight on host row. Monospace for flags.
cap: Docker offers six network modes, from the default bridge to sharing the host namespace.

name: n25-cniadd
title: What happens when a pod starts: CNI ADD
spec: Numbered steps flowing left to right. 1 'containerd or CRI-O creates the pod sandbox: a network namespace, usually held by the pause container'. 2 'runtime reads /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist and runs the plugin from /opt/cni/bin/ with CNI_COMMAND=ADD'. 3 'plugin creates a veth or macvlan, moves one end into the namespace, calls an IPAM plugin for an address (host-local, dhcp)'. 4 'on pod delete the runtime calls DEL; .conflist chains plugins in order: bridge, portmap, bandwidth, tuning'. Monospace for paths and variables. Orange on the IPAM box.
cap: The runtime calls the CNI plugin, which wires the interface into the pod namespace and asks IPAM for an address.

name: n25-crossnode
title: Pod to pod across nodes
spec: Two nodes, node 1 with pod A 10.244.1.5 and node 2 with pod B in 10.244.2.0/24. Top path 'Overlay (VXLAN, IPIP, Geneve)': packet leaves pod A through its veth, node route says 10.244.2.0/24 goes via a tunnel device (flannel.1, tunl0 or vxlan.calico), the packet is wrapped in an outer packet to node 2 which unwraps it. Bottom path 'Routed (no encapsulation)': node 1 holds route '10.244.2.0/24 via <node2 IP>' installed by static config, BIRD or the CNI daemon; needs L2 adjacency for host-gw or BGP-learned pod prefixes. Note: cloud CNIs use VPC subnet addresses routed natively. Orange tag: 'Kubernetes: pods reach all pods without NAT'.
cap: Cross-node pod traffic either rides inside an overlay tunnel or follows plain routes to the other node.

name: n26-capturepoints
title: Where to capture
spec: A path diagram: client -> client NIC -> switch (SPAN mirror/TAP) -> server NIC -> host bridge/veth -> container namespace. Numbered capture points: 1 on the host interface (post-GRO RX, pre-offload TX; offload artefacts); 2 'tcpdump -i any' (cooked SLL headers, loses VLAN and ordering details; not for exact timing); 3 inside a container namespace 'nsenter -t PID -n tcpdump'; 4 host side of bridge or veth, compare both ends; 5 switch port mirror (SPAN), ERSPAN or TAP: the truth source for the wire, mirrored traffic can be dropped under congestion; 6 kernel tracepoints pwru, kfree_skb for drop locations. Orange highlight on point 5. Green bar: 'Ask which packets you must see, then pick the closest point that sees them'.
cap: Each capture point shows a different slice of the traffic, so choose the closest point that sees what you need.

name: n26-readcapture
title: Reading a tcpdump trace
spec: The tcpdump excerpt in monospace, with brackets grouping lines: lines 1-2 'arp who-has mikado.example.com tell duplex.example.com' / 'arp reply mikado.example.com is-at 0:2:2d:b:ee:4e' = hosts finding each other's link address (green); lines 3-5 'S' / 'S ... ack 3200063166' / '. ack 1' = TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK); then 'P 1:427(426)' request and 'P 1:773(772)' response with '. ack' lines; last two lines '9 packets received by filter', '0 packets dropped by kernel' = summary (orange). Hostnames duplex.example.com.48455 and mikado.example.com.www.
anchor: ### What tcpdump shows on the wire
cap: The trace starts with ARP, then a TCP handshake, then the request and response, and ends with a filter summary.

name: n26-filters
title: Building capture filters
spec: Table of primitives in monospace with meaning: tcp = TCP packets; udp = UDP packets; ip = IPv4; ip6 = IPv6; port <port> = TCP and/or UDP to or from the port; host <host> = to or from the host; net <network> = to or from the network. Row of operators: and (both true), or (either true), ! (negates), parentheses to group. Two example commands below: 'sudo tcpdump tcp' (only TCP packets) and 'sudo tcpdump udp or port 80 or port 443' (UDP plus any packet on port 80 or 443). Footer: 'Read pcap-filter(7) for the full primitives list'.
cap: Filters are built from primitives such as tcp, host and port, joined with and, or and not.

name: n26-workflow
title: Capture-driven troubleshooting workflow
spec: Seven numbered steps in a loop-shaped list: 1 state the question precisely; 2 choose capture points (client, server, both sides of a firewall, NAT or load balancer, switch mirror); 3 write the narrowest filter (ring buffer if intermittent); 4 reproduce the problem and note times; 5 open the files together and align by time, compare what left A with what arrived at B; 6 confirm with counters and BPF tools (nstat, ss -ti, tcpretrans, tcpdrop, conntrack); 7 fix and capture again to verify. Orange example chip: 'SYN at the server with no SYN-ACK back suggests a server firewall or a full listen queue'. Green bar: 'A capture aimed at one question often answers it in a minute'.
cap: A fixed seven-step sequence turns a vague problem into a capture that answers one question.

name: n27-lab1
title: Lab 1 topology: three namespaces and a router
spec: Three namespace boxes in a row: 'hA' on the left with interface vA 10.1.0.2/24, 'r' in the middle with interfaces rA 10.1.0.1/24 and rB 10.2.0.1/24, 'hB' on the right with interface vB 10.2.0.2/24. Two veth pair links: vA-rA and vB-rB. Default routes: hA 'default via 10.1.0.1', hB 'default via 10.2.0.1'. Orange note over r: 'Why would a router refuse to pass packets even when its interfaces look correct?'. Monospace for names and addresses.
anchor: ## Lab 1: three namespaces and a router (routing, forwarding, MTU, ICMP)
cap: Two hosts in separate namespaces reach each other only through a router namespace in the middle.

name: n27-roadmap
title: The seven labs
spec: Seven numbered cards in a staircase, each one line: Lab 1 three namespaces and a router (routing, forwarding, MTU, ICMP); Lab 2 FRR in namespaces running OSPF (link state); Lab 3 leaf-spine fabric with containerlab, eBGP unnumbered, ECMP; Lab 4 EVPN-VXLAN overlay with tenant VRFs on the same fabric; Lab 5 overlays, VPNs and tunnels with namespaces; Lab 6 load balancing, anycast and failure testing; Lab 7 a validation harness (tests as code). Orange arrow from Lab 3 to Lab 4: 'underlay does not change, the overlay is a new layer on top'. Footer: 'Evidence checklist'.
cap: The labs grow from one router in namespaces to a full fabric with overlays and tests.

name: n28-evolution
title: How device management interfaces evolved
spec: Timeline left to right with six markers: 1990s SNMP (UDP 161/162; good for monitoring, poor for configuration); 1990s to now SSH/Telnet CLI screen scraping (unstructured text, fragile parsing, no transactions); 2006+ NETCONF (RFC 6241, XML over SSH port 830, transactional, YANG); 2016+ gRPC/gNMI (OpenConfig, HTTP/2 + Protocol Buffers, streaming telemetry); 2017+ RESTCONF (RFC 8040, HTTP + JSON/XML on YANG); now Linux NOS (SONiC, Cumulus, FRR). Each marker has a strength chip (green) and a weakness chip (orange). Orange note: 'A script parsing the fourth column of a CLI table breaks silently when a vendor adds a column'.
anchor: ## 2. The evolution of device management interfaces
cap: Each generation of device interface reacted to the weaknesses of the one before it.

name: n28-modeldriven
title: NETCONF, RESTCONF and gNMI compared
spec: Three-column comparison table with rows: Encoding: XML / JSON or XML / JSON, JSON_IETF or PROTO (protobuf); Transport: SSH (TLS) / HTTP(S) / gRPC over HTTP/2 + TLS; Transaction scope: network-wide capable (lock, candidate, commit) / single target, single shot / single target, Set atomic per request; Streaming telemetry: notifications (limited) / SSE (limited) / native Subscribe (sample, on-change); Tooling: ncclient / curl, requests / gNMIc, pygnmi, Telegraf; Best for: configuration with transactions / simple CRUD / high-rate telemetry. Green bar: 'Choose NETCONF when you need transactions, and gNMI for high-rate telemetry'.
cap: NETCONF suits transactional configuration, RESTCONF suits simple web tooling and gNMI suits streaming telemetry.

name: n28-sdnmodels
title: Four SDN control plane models
spec: Four rows from left (all on device) to right (all central), as a slider: Distributed: control plane runs on the forwarding devices (OSPF/IS-IS/BGP everywhere); Augmented: distributed stays, off-box processes influence the RIB (PCE, BGP controllers, Fibbing, I2RS); Hybrid: centralised control plane runs in parallel with the distributed one (controller speaking BGP/OpenFlow alongside OSPF); Replace: no distributed control plane, controller programs the FIB directly (classic OpenFlow, P4Runtime). A bar below: 'a control plane supplies topology, reachability and policy'. Orange note: 'what happens when the controller or its connectivity fails?'.
cap: The four models differ mainly in where the control plane runs.

name: n29-toolmap
title: Which tool owns which job
spec: Row of job boxes with the tools beneath each: 'Push config to existing devices' -> Ansible (agentless, YAML playbooks, idempotent modules), Nornir (Python framework, threaded runner); 'Provision cloud and controller resources' -> Terraform / OpenTofu (declarative, state, plan/apply); 'Review, test, deploy' -> Git + CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins); 'Verify before and after' -> Batfish, pyATS/Genie, Suzieq; 'Chain tickets to automation' -> StackStorm, n8n, Temporal, Airflow, ServiceNow Flow; 'Intent-based fabric operation' -> vendor controllers (Arista CloudVision, NVIDIA UFM/NetQ, Nokia EDA). Green bar: 'Write the job in one sentence; that points to one row'.
cap: Each automation tool owns a different part of the change process.

name: n29-axes
title: Axes for comparing automation tools
spec: Four small two-ended sliders, each with examples at each end. Axis 1: configuration management (converge existing machines: Ansible, Nornir) versus provisioning (create and destroy resources: Terraform). Axis 2: declarative (end state, Terraform) versus imperative (steps, scripts). Axis 3: push (central control node: Ansible, Nornir, Terraform) versus pull (ZTP, on-box agents, GitOps pull). Axis 4: mutable (change devices in place, usual for networks) versus immutable (replace a node with a new image). Orange note: 'Declarative tools depend on trustworthy diffs'.
cap: Tools differ on configuration versus provisioning, declarative versus imperative, push versus pull and mutable versus immutable.

name: n29-ansible
title: How an Ansible run works
spec: Left to right: 'control node' box containing inventory (hosts) and playbook (tasks, each calls a module). Arrow to a leaf switch. Two paths: 'Linux servers: SSH, copy a small module to the target, run it there, remove it' and 'network devices: no Python on device, so network modules run on the control node and reach the device through a connection plugin'. Final step: check whether the device now matches (idempotent), summary of which hosts changed. Monospace: 'pip install ansible-core', 'ansible-galaxy collection install arista.eos cisco.ios ansible.netcommon'.
cap: Ansible reads the inventory, runs each task's module and checks whether each device now matches.

name: n29-drift
title: Terraform and configuration drift
spec: Three panels in sequence. Panel 1 'Code says': Terraform resources google_compute_network, google_compute_subnetwork, google_compute_firewall (declarative, state recorded). Panel 2 'Someone adds a firewall rule in the console to fix something urgent' (orange, nobody writes it down): reality has drifted. Panel 3 'Months later a rebuild recreates the network from code and the rule is missing' (orange failure). Terraform bar in green: 'plan shows where reality has drifted from the code'. Footer: 'make no console-only changes'.
cap: Terraform keeps a record of what should exist and shows where reality has drifted from it.

name: n30-workflow
title: The incident workflow
spec: Seven numbered steps down the page: 1 stabilise and scope (who is affected, since when, what changed, name an incident lead); 2 define the symptom in measurable terms (example: rank 37 to rank 112 all-reduce latency rose from 1.2 ms to 40 ms starting 02:13); 3 form hypotheses, rank by likelihood and cost of testing; 4 half-split along the signal path and collect evidence; 5 manipulate to confirm the cause, simplify; 6 apply the immediate fix, verify with the purpose metric; 7 permanent fix and learning. Side notes: 'bottom-up when many things fail or after a hardware change', 'top-down when only one application misbehaves'. Orange highlight on step 2.
cap: Define the symptom in measurable terms and gather evidence before changing anything.

name: n30-kit
title: What the diagnostic kit collects
spec: A central box 'netdiag.sh: read-only collector, output tarball attached to the ticket' with eight grouped branches, each with example commands in monospace: system (date, uname, uptime); addresses and routes (ip -br addr, ip route show table all, ip rule, ip neigh); sockets (ss -s, ss -tanpi); counters (nstat -az, /proc/net/softnet_stat, /proc/net/dev); NIC (ethtool -S, -k, -g, -m); firewall (nft list ruleset, iptables-save, conntrack -S, tc -s qdisc); DNS (resolv.conf, resolvectl status); kernel logs, RDMA and GPU (dmesg, ibstat, rdma link, nvidia-smi topo -m). Green bar: 'Attach the archive to the ticket before anyone changes the node'.
cap: One scripted collector gathers the same evidence from any node in under a minute.

name: n30-pfcstorm
title: Case 8: the PFC storm
spec: A chain of four switches or ports, left to right, each sending pause frames backwards (arrows pointing right to left). Timeline strip: job runs fine for five minutes, then throughput falls to zero. Facts: ib_write_bw passes when idle; ethtool -S shows rx_pause rising by millions per second; ECN thresholds were set too high, so buffers filled before ECN or CNP could slow the sender. Resolution box in green: lower ECN thresholds below the PFC threshold, verify DCQCN on the NICs, enable the PFC watchdog, find any stuck endpoint. Bar: 'ECN must act well before PFC'.
anchor: ### Case 8: PFC storm collapses an NCCL job
cap: A pause storm spreads backwards through the fabric until throughput drops to zero, and early ECN marking prevents it.

name: n31-threequestions
title: The three questions of monitoring
spec: Three stacked questions each with checks: 1 'Is it up?' availability of devices, links, sessions and services; 2 'Is it healthy?' errors, drops, saturation, latency, temperature and power; 3 'Is it doing its job?' the purpose metric: collective bandwidth and job completion time, or inference latency and error rate (orange, start here). Right side two method chips: 'USE: utilisation, saturation, errors, for each interface and queue', 'RED: for services such as DNS, DHCP, load balancers and the monitoring pipeline'. Green bar: 'Start with the purpose metric'.
cap: Every monitoring setup should answer whether it is up, whether it is healthy and whether it is doing its job.

name: n31-signals
title: AI fabric signals and alert rules
spec: Table with columns Signal, Why it matters, Alert logic, with six example rows: per-port throughput: sustained over 85% on uplinks; egress queue occupancy: high-water mark approaching ECN/PFC thresholds; drops per queue: any drop on the lossless priority; PFC pause frames and watchdog events: pause rate above baseline, any watchdog trigger; ECN marks and CNPs: persistent high CNP rate = chronic congestion; physical layer (FEC, CRC/FCS, optics DOM): predicts failing optics before link-down; job-level (NCCL timeouts, step time): step time over baseline x 1.2. Orange on the lossless priority row. Footer: group by rail, pod, tenant and device role, compare peers.
anchor: ## 4. Signals that matter in an AI/ML fabric
cap: A few signals, each with a clear alert rule, tell you the most about an AI fabric.

name: n31-ifa
title: In-band telemetry with IFA
spec: A path across a fabric: ingress leaf (Initiator) -> spine (Transit) -> egress leaf or border (Terminator) -> collector (IPFIX). Initiator samples traffic and clones it into probe packets carrying an IFA header, initiator tag, timestamps. Transit nodes append device ID, ingress and egress ports, queue ID, ingress timestamp, residence time in nanoseconds, congestion bit when ECN marking applies.
